title: Alba and the Cathedral's Crack
markdown:
Alba, the Snow Weaver, lived in a tower that scraped the stars. Its spires were filigree of solidified moonlight and icicles that sang when winter breathed. His beard, a cascade of hoarfrost, tickled his knees while he watched snowflakes decide where to land. He liked the hush before a storm woke.

The sky churned. Not gentle snow: a roaring tempest. Wind howled. Rain, sharp as needles, lashed the crystalline walls. A tremor ran through him — not panic, concern. Far below, a legend of the world was in trouble.

The dome of Florence Cathedral, Brunelleschi’s marvel, was groaning. A colossal stone spine, a hundred dizzying feet in the air, had sprung a ravenous fissure. It threatened to shatter the heart of the city’s soaring edifice.

“A crack,” Alba murmured, a chime of breaking ice. He peered through a frost-rimmed window, glacial eyes narrowing. “Unacceptable.”

A blur of dark determined feathers zipped through a gap. Pipit, chimney swift, landed on the icy desk and shook droplets from stormy-grey wings. “Alba! A proper fright out there. The old dome’s groaning like a giant who’s stubbed his toe.”

Alba’s eyes met Pipit’s bright worried ones. “You have seen this crack?”

“Seen it? Felt it.” Pipit puffed his chest. “The wind nearly tossed me into the Arno. Old stories say Brunelleschi used clever tricks. He didn’t just stack stones. He understood how they hold together.”

Alba rose with the rustle of a winter wind. He did not offer a proverb about true strength. He reached for his starlight shawl, a shimmer of cosmic dust and frozen light. “Then we fly. Quickly.”

Pipit perched on his shoulder. Together they soared into the tempest, frost and feathers against a bruised sky. The wind tried to tear them apart. The rain stung like icy pebbles. Purpose, at least, did not flap away.

They landed with a soft thud on the storm-lashed roof. Tiles under Alba’s boots had become treacherous glass. Ozone, metallic and bitter, mixed with wet stone. The wind screamed and clawed at the shawl.

“That crack!” Pipit pointed a trembling wing. “It’s widening.”

Alba raised ancient hands. The first wisps of snow already dusted his fingers. The stone trembled, a deep resonating complaint. His magic could freeze, solidify, make things brittle. Here he needed to mend, not shatter.

“The weight is immense,” he admitted. “I can freeze the crack. Make it solid. The pressure might just push through.”

Pipit darted closer, a small frantic rhythm against Alba’s tunic. “Don’t just freeze it. Remember Brunelleschi. Tension. How the whole structure works as one.”

The words were a spark in the roaring dark. Alba closed his eyes and pictured the dome not as stones but as a single breathing thing. He was a keeper of stillness. Stillness, properly used, could hold.

He drew in the storm’s raw power and shaped it. For a heart-stopping moment nothing happened. The wind howled its defiance. Rain lashed. Pipit braced, tiny body trembling.

Alba reached out. A shimmering crystalline thread, stronger than steel, finer than spider’s silk, wove from his fingertips and dove into the crack. It pulsed frosty blue and smelled of frozen mountain air. The cathedral’s pressure pressed down, an avalanche of stars. Pipit’s warmth against the frigid cloak was unexpected and useful. Alba channelled every ounce, not to shatter, but to bind.

Then, with a final surge drawn from the storm itself, the icy thread pulsed and sealed the fracture. The dome’s groan lessened. Profound quiet replaced it. The wind sighed, rage spent. Rain softened, then ceased, a gentle patter that was almost polite.

Alba slumped, breathless. Pipit chirped and fluttered around his head. The magnificent dome stood against the retreating weather.

“We did it, Pipit.”

“We did.” Pipit landed on the frosty beard, a speck of vibrant life against settled cold. He did not add a speech about buildings and friendships. Dawn, shy, painted the wet rooftops rosy-gold. Alba and Pipit sat on the tiles and listened to the dome not groan. That, for a stormy night, was the whole of the music.
